opus-5.5.text:
I think, looking back, it was a very generous decision, and honestly not one every advisor would make. MSRA at that time was kind of the obvious, prestigious choice. For a student in China doing computer vision, it was almost the default path, and a lot of people would say, "Why would you go anywhere else?" So for Professor Yu to say, "Okay, if this is what you want, go try it," that took a certain openness.

What I appreciate most is that he didn't treat it as a matter of whose name was on the internship or what looked best on paper. He respected that I had my own curiosity and my own sense of direction, even though at that age I probably couldn't fully explain why I wanted it. I just had this feeling that I wanted to see something different, to be in a new environment and get out of my comfort zone a bit.

And I think that kind of trust matters a lot for a young researcher. When someone gives you room to make your own choice, you also feel responsible for it. You can't blame anyone else if it doesn't work out, so you push yourself harder to make it worthwhile.

Of course, I can't say for sure what would have happened if I had gone to MSRA. Maybe that would have been a great path too. But that experience taught me something I still carry with me now, especially as I work with my own students: often the best thing a mentor can do is not to pick the "optimal" route for you, but to protect your ability to explore and make your own decisions. That freedom, in the long run, shapes you more than any single opportunity.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think that was one of the most generous things anyone did for me early on, and I didn't fully appreciate it at the time.

The context was that I was an undergraduate at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, in the ACM class, and the natural path for someone like me was MSRA. Professor Yu Yong had very close ties there, and almost everyone in our program who wanted to do research went through that door. It was the prestigious option, the "correct" option. And Professor Yu could have easily just said, go to MSRA, this is the path, don't overthink it.

But I had this somewhat irrational pull toward going to Singapore. Part of it was that I wanted to work on something a bit different from what everyone around me was doing, and part of it was honestly just that I was young and wanted to see somewhere new. If you had asked me to justify it on paper, I don't think I could have made a compelling case against MSRA.

What struck me was that he didn't try to talk me out of it. He asked me why I wanted to go, listened, and then basically said, if this is what you want, go do it, and I'll support you. He didn't make me feel like I was wasting an opportunity or being ungrateful for the connections he'd built.

I think that reflects something about how he thought about mentorship. He understood that a student's trajectory isn't something you optimize from the outside. The thing that actually matters is whether the student is excited and engaged, because that's where the real work comes from. A slightly less prestigious internship that I was genuinely motivated by was worth more than a perfect one I'd been pushed into.

And in hindsight it worked out. That experience shaped how I approached problems later, and it gave me a bit of independence early, which I think I needed. But even if it hadn't worked out, I'd still view his decision the same way. He gave me room to make my own choice and own the consequences. Now that I have my own students, I find myself trying to do the same thing, and I realize how hard it actually is to hold back when you think you know the better path.
